extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of English drama and literary criticism (Ben Jonson / Jacobean comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing or analysing comic drama in the Jonsonian/Jacobean tradition — especially the 'comedy of humours', satirical technique, characterisation, and dramatic construction. Emphasises classical precedent, caricature, and realistic drawing from contemporary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy of humours (ruling-trait characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humour, according to Jonson, was a bias of disposition, a warp ... by which 'Some one peculiar quality Doth so possess a man, that it doth draw All his affects, his spirits, and his powers, In their confluctions, all to run one way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive stage personages on the basis of a ruling trait or passion; place these typified traits in juxtaposition in their conflict and contrast to generate comedy. Examples: Downright as a 'plain squire'; Bobadill the braggart-coward; Brainworm the schemer who is fooled. Note the simplification of actual life implicit in this method; use it to heighten comic effect rather than mimic full psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid degrading the humour into mere eccentricity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'But that a rook by wearing a pied feather, The cable hat-band, or the three-piled ruff... should affect a humour! O, it is more than most ridiculous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce a character’s 'humour' to superficial oddities of dress, speech, or manner (an 'oddity of speech, an eccentricity of manner, of dress, or cut of beard'). The ruling trait should shape actions and motives, not be only a costume or catchphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical restraint and precedent (studied professionalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson was a classicist: he believed in restraint and precedent in art ... he believed that there was a professional way of doing things which might be reached by a study of the best examples, and he found these examples for the most part among the ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical models, discipline, and study as a basis for comic composition: attention to form, proportion, and authoritative examples. This is not slavish imitation — Jonson himself allowed licence — but an informed, professional practice grounded in precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance licence with formal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I see not then, but we should enjoy the same licence, or free power to illustrate and heighten our invention as they [the ancients] did; and not be tied to those strict and regular forms which the niceness of a few, who are nothing but form, would thrust upon us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While valuing classical models, allow dramatic freedom where it better serves invention and stage needs. Don't be rigidly bound to unities or classical constraints if creative effect requires deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of satirical attack: general vs personal
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's comedies contain two kinds of attack, the critical or generally satiric, levelled at abuses and corruptions in the abstract; and the personal, in which specific application is made of all this in the lampooning of poets and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether satire addresses societal/abstract abuses (safer, more universal) or specific contemporaries (sharper but riskier). Personal lampooning can provoke quarrels and legal trouble (as in the 'poetomachia'); use with care and awareness of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate dramatic lampoon to an art (caricature + structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: What Jonson really did, was to raise the dramatic lampoon to an art, and make out of a casual burlesque and bit of mimicry a dramatic satire of literary pretensions and permanency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform caricature and mimicry into sustained dramatic satire by embedding individual targets in a coherent plot and by giving them theatrical and rhetorical weight; satire should serve drama, not be mere skit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, observed characterisation drawn from life
rubrics_metrics.description: The play is admirably written and each character is vividly conceived, and with a firm touch based on observation of the men of the London of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground comic characters in careful observation of real social types; vividness and authenticity in depiction enhance comic impact. Use local manners, speech, and social detail to make caricature credible and resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of character can outweigh weak plot
rubrics_metrics.description: As to plot, it tells little more than ... The real quality of this comedy is in its personages and in the theory upon which they are conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comedy, striking, well-drawn characters and a strong governing idea (e.g., a ruling humour) can compensate for a simple or thin plot. Evaluate plays by characterisation and thematic coherence as well as narrative complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingenious construction and escalation (dramatic engineering)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Alchemist' Jonson represented ... the whole fabric building climax on climax, witty, ingenious, and so plausibly presented that we forget its departures from the possibilities of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft scenes and devices so that action escalates logically toward theatrical climaxes; manage pacing and revelation so the audience accepts even improbable devices. Constructional cleverness is a key measure of comic success (examples: The Silent Woman's central joke; The Alchemist's progressive deceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of antimasque and contrast in masque structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson invented the antimasque, a comedy or farcical element of relief, entrusted to professional players or dancers, enhancing the beauty and dignity of the masque portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In courtly spectacle or mixed-genre pieces, alternate serious masque sequences with antimasque comic relief to provide tonal balance and heightened effect; comic interludes should contrast, not undermine, the main ceremonial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism of urban life enhances satirical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In his comedies of London life, despite his trend towards caricature, Jonson has shown himself a genuine realist, drawing from the life about him with an experience and insight rare in any generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic depiction of contemporary urban manners and institutions strengthens satire and comedy; specificity (e.g., types at Bartholomew Fair) provides material for both ridicule and pathos. Comparison to Dickens implies moral, social depth beneath the humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and rhetorical style: trenchant wit and invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's uncommon eloquence in scorn, vituperation, and invective ... couched in witty and brilliant dialogue and sustained by that righteous indignation which must lie at the heart of all true satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of comic writing by its verbal brilliance and rhetorical force—wit, scorn, and sustained indignation can power satire. But weigh eloquence against fairness and theatrical effect; excess can alienate audiences or provoke retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of Rabelaisian excess and loosening of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in 'Bartholomew Fair' that the humour of Jonson, always open to this danger, loosens into the Rabelaisian mode ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that satire and caricature can tip into grotesque excess, losing control and becoming coarser than intended; recognise when exuberance undermines subtlety or audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral stance and the poet as moralist
rubrics_metrics.description: Both [Jonson and Dickens] were at heart moralists, seeking the truth by the exaggerated methods of humour and caricature; perverse, even wrong-headed at times, but possessed of a true pathos and largeness of heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether comic works embody a moral purpose or corrective intent; satire’s value is often judged by its moral seriousness and capacity to leave the audience 'better' for the art, not merely amused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erudition and learned source-use as dramatic resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson was a scholar and a classical antiquarian ... he reprobated slipshod amateurishness, and wrote his 'Sejanus' like a scholar, reading Tacitus, Suetonius, and other authorities, to be certain of his facts, his setting, and his atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use researched historical or classical material to lend authority and texture to plays; learned allusion can enrich satire and give weight to comic inversions, though overly pedantic display risks alienating readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of scene/locale to serve the comic aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Our scene is London, 'cause we would make known No country's mirth is better than our own.' ... Jonson transferred scenes to London to make national commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select setting deliberately to foreground local social satire or national comedy. Adapting scene to audience expectations (e.g., setting in London) can increase immediacy and satirical force.
